title: Retired Cop Jailed Over Charlie Kirk Meme Wins $835,000 Free Speech Settlement
summary: When Larry Bushart posted a meme on Facebook, he never imagined it would land him in jail for over a month. But the 61-year-old retired police officer from Tennessee became a rare example of criminal prosecution over online speech — and now he's won an $835,000 settlement. The meme that sparked the case featured President Donald Trump and the words, "We have to get over it," a quote Trump made after a 2024 school shooting in Perry, Iowa. Bushart captioned it, "This seems relevant today..." in the wake of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk's killing, which had prompted an outpouring of grief. In Perry County, Tennessee, near Bushart's home, residents were alarmed. They feared the post threatened a local school, also named Perry County High School. Sheriff Nick Weems acknowledged most of Bushart's "hate memes" were lawful free speech but said investigators believed Bushart "intentionally sought to create hysteria." Bushart was arrested in September on a felony charge. His bail was set at $2 million. During his 37 days behind bars, he lost his post-retirement job, missed his wedding anniversary, and wasn't there for his granddaughter's birth. In October, authorities dropped the charge. Bushart then filed a federal lawsuit, arguing his First Amendment rights were violated. On Wednesday, the settlement was announced. "The people's freedom to participate in civil discourse is crucial to a healthy democracy," Bushart said. His attorney, Cary Davis of the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, added: "It's in times of turmoil and heightened tensions that our national commitment to free speech is tested the most. When government officials fail that test, the Constitution exists to hold them accountable." The case raises thorny questions: When does provocative speech cross the line into a true threat? And how should law enforcement balance public fear with constitutional rights? For Bushart, the answer came with a price tag — and a warning to officials nationwide.
why_it_matters: This case highlights the uneasy line between public safety and free expression in the digital age. When officials misread an ambiguous online post, innocent people can lose their freedom, and that can have a chilling effect on the kind of open debate that a healthy democracy needs.

background_read: Larry Bushart’s meme featured Donald Trump (the U.S. president from 2017–2021 and again since 2025) with the quote ‘We have to get over it,’ originally said by Trump after a school shooting in Perry, Iowa. The post appeared in the wake of the killing of Charlie Kirk, a well-known conservative activist and media personality.

Perry County, Tennessee, where Bushart lives, is a small, rural county. A local school shares the name ‘Perry County High School,’ which led some residents to connect the post to a threat against their own community — even though Bushart’s meme came from a different Perry, in Iowa. This confusion fueled the panic.

The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) is a non-profit legal group that specialises in defending free speech on college campuses and beyond. It often takes cases where public officials may have overstepped constitutional boundaries.

U.S. courts allow prosecution for ‘true threats’ — statements that a reasonable person would view as a serious expression of intent to harm — but social media posts can easily be misinterpreted. Similar cases, such as the 2014 arrest of a teenager for a Facebook comment about a school, reveal how local authorities sometimes rush to charge individuals over ambiguous online speech.

Bushart’s $2 million bail and 37 days in jail are unusually severe for a speech-related charge, especially given that the post did not contain a direct threat. The settlement amount of $835,000 is meant to compensate him and deter future First Amendment violations by officials.

perspectives.description: The settlement sends a powerful message that the First Amendment still protects unpopular or provocative speech. It deters local police and prosecutors from rushing to arrest people over social media posts that, however distasteful, are not true threats.

Some officers and community members genuinely feared the post was a warning of an imminent school attack. In an era of frequent school shootings, overreacting can be preferable to underreacting, and a large settlement may make law enforcement hesitate to act when real threats do appear.

The case fits a recurring pattern in U.S. courts: officials apply broad ‘true threat’ standards to social media content without considering ambiguity of tone, audience misunderstanding, or the poster’s intent. The legal precedent from this settlement is limited, but it illustrates how costly such misjudgments can be.

The outcome may encourage police departments to seek clearer guidelines on investigating online speech. Future training could focus on distinguishing hyperbolic or satirical posts from genuine threats, and courts may eventually refine the ‘true threat’ test for social media to better protect both public safety and civil liberties.
